# Keel — full documentation for retrieval

> The SQLite of durable execution: production-grade resilience and opt-in durable
> execution as an in-process library, zero code changes, policy in one
> `keel.toml`. This file is the self-contained corpus — every feature with one
> canonical example, plus the CLI and error-code reference. Stable headings; an
> agent can retrieve any section without following a link.

## What Keel is

Keel wraps a program's outbound effects at the call boundary and applies a
policy: retries, exponential backoff with jitter, per-attempt timeouts, circuit
breakers, rate limits, response caching, and — opt-in — crash-resumable durable
flows. It runs inside your process (no daemon, no port, no login); state is files
under `.keel/`. Add it with `keel run`; remove the package and your code runs
identically (minus resilience). Two tiers:

- **Tier 1 (resilience):** always on, per intercepted call. cache → rate →
  breaker → timeout → retry.
- **Tier 2 (durability):** opt-in per flow. Journals each effect; a crashed run
  re-executes from the top and substitutes already-completed effects from the
  journal instead of re-firing them.

## The "just works" ladder

### Level 0 — zero config

```
keel run app.py            # python
keel run app.mjs           # node
```

Every discovered outbound call gets conservative production defaults (30s
timeout, 3 retries on transient errors — conn/timeout/429/5xx — with jittered
exponential backoff, per-host breaker). LLM provider calls get the LLM pack. One
line of output, then silence. Hard rules: never change success-path semantics;
never retry a non-idempotent call (POST without an idempotency key) by default —
it is marked observed-not-retried (KEEL-E014); if Keel can't wrap something
safely it does nothing and says so in `keel doctor`.

### Level 1 — `keel init`

```
keel init                  # writes keel.toml from static scan + observed runs
keel init --diff           # preview adds/removes against an existing keel.toml
```

Generated entries cite `file:line` evidence and observed traffic; deleting any
entry falls back to the same built-in defaults. The generated file is the
documentation.

### Level 2 — durable flows (config-only)

```toml
# keel.toml
[flows]
entrypoints = ["py:pipeline:main"]     # module `pipeline`, function `main`
```

```
keel run pipeline.py       # runs it as a durable flow
# kill -9 it mid-run, then re-run: resumes, replaying completed steps
```

Completed steps are substituted from `.keel/journal.db` (their effects never
re-fire); the rest run live. `keel flows` lists resumable/completed flows;
`keel trace <flow>` shows the step ledger. Time (`time.time`/`time_ns`) and
`random.random` reads inside a flow are virtualized so a resumed run sees the
same values.

Limits (precise, never silent): a flow needs a journal (native core).
Async flow bodies are supported: an `async def` entrypoint's awaited
intercepted calls route through the same open flow handle as a synchronous
flow's, journaled identically; concurrent awaited effects (`asyncio.gather`)
are admitted — and journaled — in the order their calls reach the handle,
never in completion order.

### Level 3 — fleet

One line (`journal = "postgres://…"`) moves the journal to Postgres for
multi-process, cross-host fleet recovery; nothing else changes. Lease
arbitration reads the DATABASE's clock, not any one process's, so it stays
correct under host clock drift.

## Targets

A policy entry is `[target."<key>"]`. Kinds:

- **host** — e.g. `[target."api.stripe.com"]`, matched by request host.
- **`py:` / `ts:` functions** — e.g. `[target."py:pipeline.do_step"]`; listing a
  function asserts it is safe to retry (idempotent).
- **semantic** — `llm:<provider>` (openai/anthropic/google-genai/…),
  `tool:<name>`, `mcp:<server>`. Auto-detected from provider hosts / framework
  adapters.
- **`cmd:<name>`** — an external command dispatched as a journaled Tier-2
  durable flow, matched on argv under `[flows.match."cmd:<name>"]` (prefix
  match: the observed argv must be at least as long as the declared pattern,
  trailing args unconstrained).
- **route key** — a key carrying a method and a path, e.g.
  `[target."POST *-aiplatform.googleapis.com/*:fetchPredictOperation"]`. It is
  matched on method, host, effective port and path, and it beats Keel's own
  LLM host-map classification for that route, so a status-poll route can carry
  its own timeout, breaker and poll policy while the chat route keeps the LLM
  pack. A host-only glob is NOT a route key and never captures LLM traffic.

Canonical policy example:

```toml
[target."api.stripe.com"]              # seen in: billing.py:41
retry       = { attempts = 5, schedule = "exp(200ms, x2, max 30s, jitter)" }
idempotency = { header = "Idempotency-Key" }

[target."llm:openai"]                   # seen in: agent.py:12
retry = { attempts = 6, on = ["429","5xx","timeout"] }
rate  = "60/min"
cache = { mode = "dev" }                # dev-loop cache; inert when KEEL_ENV=prod
```

## Resilience features (one example each)

- **Retry + backoff:** `retry = { attempts = 5, schedule = "exp(200ms, x2, max 30s, jitter)", on = ["conn","timeout","429","5xx"] }`. 429 backoff honors `Retry-After` when larger than the scheduled wait.
- **Timeout:** `timeout = "30s"` — enforced per attempt (KEEL-E011 on breach).
- **Circuit breaker:** `breaker = { failures = 5, cooldown = "15s" }` — opens after N failures, half-opens after cooldown (KEEL-E012 while open).
- **Rate limit:** `rate = "60/min"` — token bucket; KEEL-E013 if the wait budget is exceeded.
- **Idempotency:** `idempotency = { header = "Idempotency-Key" }` — makes a non-idempotent call retryable (otherwise KEEL-E014, observed-not-retried).
- **Cache / LLM dev-cache:** `cache = { mode = "dev" }` — identical request+args replay off `KEEL_ENV=prod`; with the native core + journal it persists across separate runs (a repeated prompt costs ~0). `cache = { mode = "off" }` disables caching for a target outright. The dev cache is also off by default on serverless platforms, and never derives a key for a streaming (`text/event-stream`) or long-running-operation-shaped call.
- **Poll until terminal:** `poll = { interval = "10s", deadline = "30m", until = { field = "status", terminal = ["succeeded", "failed"] } }` — turns a submit-then-poll long-running operation into one awaited call. Poll wraps retry, so each probe still retries; cache, rate and breaker see one logical call. `until.field` may be a dotted path (`response.state`) and `until.terminal` matches by JSON type, so `"true"` and `true` are distinguishable. KEEL-E016 when the deadline runs out. The gate is idempotency, not method: any call Keel judges idempotent can be polled, which includes Google `:fetch*Operation` POSTs (see below) — scope the poll with a route key if that is broader than you want.
- **`until.absent` — the missing-field rule (CCR-11):** a parsed JSON object that does not carry `until.field` is neither terminal nor pending until you say which. (A response Keel cannot parse into a JSON object at all — a 502 HTML page, a bodyless envelope, an undecodable body — fails open before `until` is consulted, regardless of `absent`.) `absent = "fail_open"` is the default and the behavior of every policy written before CCR-11: return the body unchanged and end the poll. `absent = "pending"` treats the absence as the pending signal and keeps polling. **Set it for every `google.longrunning.Operation` route** — Vertex `:fetchPredictOperation`, the Gemini API `operations/*` route, Cloud Speech, Document AI — because proto3 JSON omits a false bool, so a running body is literally `{"name": "projects/…/operations/…"}` and `done` appears only on completion:

  ```toml
  [target."POST *-aiplatform.googleapis.com/*:fetchPredictOperation"]
  timeout = "30s"
  poll    = { interval = "10s", deadline = "10m", until = { field = "done", terminal = [true], absent = "pending" } }
  ```

  Without `absent = "pending"` that block validates, attributes the calls to the route in `keel status`, and returns the first running body on attempt one — it never polls (issue #128). The default is deliberately unchanged: on a host-level `poll` table a mistyped `until.field` must not turn every ordinary response into a poll loop. `absent` is optional and accepts only those two words; anything else is KEEL-E001 at configure. It is new in 0.7.0, and an older Keel rejects the unknown key with KEEL-E001 too — under `.pth`/`--import` auto-activation that means the process runs with no Keel at all, so upgrade every process that reads this `keel.toml` before adding the key. `keel doctor`'s `hand-rolled-poll` fix emits `absent = "pending"` in its Google proposals and deliberately does not in the OpenAI/Anthropic ones, whose status bodies always carry the field. Google's two generative-AI surfaces — Vertex AI and the Gemini Developer API — share one SDK and therefore one target name, so doctor infers which one the project uses (statically, from the hosts its `keel.toml` names and the scan sighted) and proposes only that route's block; it proposes both, each noting which to delete, only when it detects neither. If the project already declares one of those route keys and its `poll.until` has no `absent`, doctor says the block does not poll and the patch amends it in place rather than going silent (issue #139).
- **Operation reads:** a `POST` to a host under `googleapis.com` whose last path segment is a `:fetch…Operation` custom method is judged idempotent without an idempotency key — re-issuing it is exactly what polling does. It is retried under Level 0 defaults and gets the per-attempt `timeout`, identically in Python, Node and Rust. The submit side (`:predictLongRunning`) is untouched and stays non-idempotent.
- **Fallback:** `fallback = ["llm:anthropic", …]` on an LLM target — after the primary's retries are exhausted, the call is re-judged and re-dispatched at the next provider, each hop under its own target's policy.

## LLM / agent frameworks

`llm:<provider>` calls get a default pack (retry on 429/5xx/timeout with
provider-aware backoff, rate limiting, dev cache). Framework adapter packs are
auto-detected from dependencies (AI SDK middleware, `mcp:` transports, etc.) and
wrap tool/LLM calls with zero agent-code changes. See dx-spec §4.

Google ADK + `agents-cli` quickstart: README's "Keel for Google ADK +
agents-cli" section (`uv add keelrun` or the `agents-cli scaffold create
my-agent -a MisterTK/keel/packaging/agents-cli-template` template, `KEEL_ENABLE=1`, `keel
init` into the agent directory). `demos/adk-demo` runs a real `LlmAgent`
riding out a 429 storm below the agent loop, and `skills/keel/` (`npx skills
add MisterTK/keel`) is the coding-agent skill.

Two more ADK-specific capabilities, both farm-certified against the real
`google-adk` package: durable, crash-resumable agent turns — designate
`py:google.adk.runners:Runner.run_async` under `[flows] entrypoints` (one
flow per process in v1; see `docs/targeting.md` for the full limitations
list) — and cross-model fallback that survives a provider switch — set
`fallback = [...]` on `llm:google-genai`; the plugin's `on_model_error` hook
resolves and constructs the fallback model via ADK's own `LLMRegistry`,
unlike the generic host/fetch seam's same-provider-only model rewrite.

## CLI reference

Global: `--json` on any command emits deterministic JSON (sorted keys, no
timestamps) instead of prose. Same command, two audiences.

- `keel run <target> [args...]` — run a script/package/dir under Keel. `--disable` runs it byte-identically with Keel off.
- `keel init [--diff] [--stamp] [--agents]` — generate `keel.toml` from evidence; `--diff` previews; `--stamp` dates the header; `--agents` writes the Keel section into `AGENTS.md` instead.
- `keel doctor [--effective-policy]` — the honesty report: what's wrapped, what's visible-but-unwrapped and why, adapter version pins, policy validity, journal backend. `--effective-policy` prints the composed `defaults < packs < user` policy `keel_configure` actually receives.
- `keel status` — coverage %, retries saved this week, breaker events, cache hit rate, resumable flows, and the last recorded activation.
- `keel report [--out PATH] [--open] [--watch] [--serve] [--port N]` — render `keel status` + the newest run's events + flows into one self-contained HTML file at `.keel/report.html`. `--watch` rewrites it on an interval; `--serve` serves it on 127.0.0.1. `--json` prints the report's data blob instead.
- `keel exec -- <command...>` — wrap one external command as a journaled Tier-2 durable flow (CCR-4): at-most-once dispatch per identity, crash-safe retry gating, and a declared-side-effect gate (KEEL-E033). NOT exactly-once execution inside the child.
- `keel explain <KEEL-E0NN>` — the exact what/why/next for an error code.
- `keel flows [--dead]` — list durable flows (id, entrypoint, status, steps, age).
- `keel flows suggest` — analyze candidate flow entrypoints for replay-safety (effect counts, idempotent-unsafe effects, time/random reads, an estimated replay-safe verdict).
- `keel flows add <entrypoint> [--diff]` — designate an entrypoint as a durable flow: appends it to `[flows] entrypoints`, idempotent re-run.
- `keel flows resume [<flow> | --all]` — re-invoke a resumable flow's recorded entrypoint through `keel run`.
- `keel flows force <flow>` — arm the durable one-shot KEEL-E033 override: the next re-dispatch that would otherwise be refused because the declared side-effect files changed proceeds exactly once, then the override clears itself. The out-of-process, config-free equivalent of `keel exec --force`.
- `keel trace <flow>` — one flow's steps (outcomes, attempts, timings).
- `keel replay <flow> [--step N]` — a journal-driven dry run of what re-entering the flow would do: which steps substitute, which re-execute, where replay resumes.
- `keel tail [--run ID] [--no-follow]` — live view of attempts/backoffs/breaker transitions while a program runs, reading `.keel/events/`; no daemon.
- `keel fsck [--fix] [--prune AGE]` — journal integrity check (orphan steps, dangling leases, expired cache), safe repairs, and retention pruning.
- `keel mcp` — serve this project over MCP on stdio (JSON-RPC 2.0; no daemon, exits on EOF). Six tools: `get_status`, `get_doctor_report`, `propose_policy` (returns a keel.toml diff), `get_trace`, `list_flows`, `explain_error`. Each tool's text result is byte-identical to the matching command's `--json` output.
- `keel record run <target> [args...]` / `keel record list` / `keel record test <recording>` — capture every intercepted effect during a run into `.keel/recordings/`, then turn a recording into a replayable offline test fixture (a pytest fixture or `node:test` file) that fails loudly on any unmatched effect.
- `keel sim <plan>` — replay a declarative fault plan (injected errors, latency, crash-restart points) against a script or a recording, asserting the policy holds (retries within budget, breaker opens as configured, flows resume). Adapter-level fault injection, not hermetic simulation.

## Observability

Silence on success is a DX invariant, not a lack of evidence:

- **Exit summary** — every run ends with one screen: calls, retries, cache
  hits, breaker trips, unprotected calls (with the top targets named), and
  any runtime suspicions such as `cache-poll-suspect` (5 consecutive cache
  hits on one identical key spanning ≥20s — the shape of a poll loop being
  replayed).
- **`keel report`** — the same evidence as a self-contained HTML page, live
  with `--watch` or `--serve`.
- **`KEEL_LOG_FORMAT=json`** — five deployment-evidence lines become one JSON
  object per line, byte-identical between Python and Node: the startup
  (activation) line, the exit summary, BOTH activation refusals
  (`policy-missing-at-keel-cwd`, and `activation-failed` for any other
  bootstrap failure — including a `keel.toml` an older Keel cannot parse), the
  ephemeral-journal warning, and the `cache-poll-suspect` warning. Every one
  of them carries a `severity` (`INFO` on the activation and summary,
  `WARNING` on the two warnings, `ERROR` on both refusals) — Cloud Logging and
  CloudWatch fill an entry's severity only from that field, so without it a
  refusal to activate is indistinguishable from a healthy start in any
  `severity>=ERROR` view. Nothing else converts: other `keel ▸ …` prose stays
  prose. Use it in containers.
- **`keel tail`** — attempts, backoffs and breaker transitions as they
  happen, read from `.keel/events/`. No daemon.
- **`KEEL_EVENTS=stderr`** — writes the same NDJSON event feed to the
  process's stderr instead of `.keel/events/<run>.ndjson`. On Cloud Run, GKE
  and Lambda stderr already is the log pipeline, so this is per-attempt
  evidence off the instance with no collector, no volume and no custom build.
  Limits, stated plainly: it is **native-core only** (the pure-Python and JS
  fallback backends have no event sink to redirect); the feed then shares fd 2
  with Keel's own console output and nothing coordinates the two streams, so
  a consumer distinguishes them by the event lines' fixed `v`/`seq`/`ms`/
  `event` keys; and `keel tail` has no on-disk feed to follow (it says so
  rather than claiming there are no events), while `keel report` renders with
  an empty event stream. This is a step toward a real remote evidence sink,
  not that sink (issue #94 stays open).
- **OpenTelemetry** is opt-in and build-time: the `otel` cargo feature plus
  `KEEL_OTEL=1`. It is NOT enabled in any published package.

## Dependency activation (without `keel run`)

When another tool owns the process (test runners, `agents-cli`, `adk api_server`, uvicorn), activate Keel via environment variables:

- **Python**: the `keelrun` wheel ships a `.pth` shim gated on `KEEL_ENABLE=1`. Set it in your `.env` and every Python process boots with the same policy engine as `keel run` — loading `keel.toml` from the working directory, or from `KEEL_CWD=<dir>` when config lives in the deployable app. `KEEL_DISABLE=1` always wins.
- **Node**: add `NODE_OPTIONS="--import keelrun/register"` alongside `KEEL_ENABLE=1`. Same `KEEL_ENABLE` gate as Python, and Node honors `KEEL_CWD` too — both front ends read `keel.toml` from the working directory and both relocate that root when `KEEL_CWD` is set.
- **`KEEL_CWD` is an assertion, not a hint.** If it names a directory with no `keel.toml`, Keel prints `keel ▸ error: KEEL_CWD=… is set but …/keel.toml does not exist — Keel NOT activated` and the host runs keel-free; `keel run` exits 2 instead. `KEEL_POLICY=optional` restores the older behavior of running Level 0 defaults with a warning. Without `KEEL_CWD`, a missing `keel.toml` still means Level 0 defaults, and the banner names the directory it searched (and any `keel.toml` found above it).
- Activation is fail-open for the host: a broken install or invalid `keel.toml` prints one `keel ▸` line; your app runs unwrapped. The preflight resilience advisory stays a `keel run`-only, CLI-side feature in both languages. Python's `.pth` shim additionally skips `keel record` / `keel sim` wiring and flow-entrypoint dispatch (designated via `[flows] entrypoints`, not auto-detected). Node's `keelrun/register` is a thin `KEEL_ENABLE` gate around the same preload `keel run` uses — flow-entrypoint dispatch and `KEEL_RECORD`/`KEEL_SIM_PLAN` wiring behave exactly as under `keel run`.
- **Deployment honesty.** On a serverless platform (`K_SERVICE`, `AWS_LAMBDA_FUNCTION_NAME`, …) the default LLM dev cache is off unless `KEEL_ENV=dev` says otherwise, and a SQLite journal on ephemeral storage draws a runtime warning plus a `journal-ephemeral-storage` doctor finding. `keel doctor` reads a root `Dockerfile` for `COPY keel.toml` (`keel-toml-not-in-image`), and every activation writes an evidence row that `keel status` / `keel report` show and `keel doctor --json` reports as `runtime_activation: "verified" | "unverified"`, alongside `activation_backend: "native" | "stub" | null` — which backend that verifying activation actually ran on (`null` when unverified, or when the row predates the column). `keel status` names it on the last-activation line too. `keel doctor --json` also carries `llm_surfaces`, keyed by target — `{"llm:google-genai": {"detected": ["vertex"], "source": "policy" | "static" | "none", "evidence": [hosts]}}` — the static Google-surface verdict described above; the key is omitted entirely when there is nothing to report. There is deliberately no `"runtime"` source: Keel discards the host at target resolution, so which surface a project actually *called* never reaches the discovery store or the events feed (issue #140).
- **Backend selection (Python only).** `KEEL_BACKEND` defaults to `auto`, which tries the native core first and silently falls back to a pure-Python backend whenever the native module fails to import — a real production degradation path, not just a dev convenience. The pure-Python backend gives you Tier 1 resilience (retry/timeout/breaker/rate/cache/poll) with a real wall clock, but no Tier 2 durable flows and no cross-run cache persistence (the process-lifetime cache still works). The activation banner names it explicitly (`pure-Python backend: no durable flows, no cross-run cache`) and the JSON summary's `backend` field reports `"native"` or the fallback's name, so which backend actually ran is never silent. `KEEL_BACKEND=native` makes the missing module a hard failure (KEEL-E005) instead of a silent fallback; `KEEL_BACKEND=stub` forces the pure-Python backend even when native is available. Node has the same three-way `KEEL_BACKEND` selection and the same auto-fallback shape (to an in-process JS engine), but its native addon ships prebuilt on npm, so falling back is rare in practice rather than a routine deploy hazard. Both languages report the resolved backend the same way: the activation JSON and the JSON summary each carry a `backend` field.

## Error codes (frozen taxonomy)

Every user-facing error carries a `KEEL-E0NN` code, a first line (what/why/next),
a `--json` twin, and a trace reference. `keel explain <code>` prints the detail.

- KEEL-E001 policy-invalid — keel.toml failed validation (wrong type / unknown key / bad literal). Next: `keel doctor`; validate against policy.schema.json.
- KEEL-E002 policy-target-unknown — strict mode only; unknown target with no entry.
- KEEL-E003 envelope-decode — a request/attempt-result envelope could not be decoded at the FFI boundary (version mismatch / corruption).
- KEEL-E004 envelope-version-unsupported — language package and core binary are incompatible releases.
- KEEL-E005 unsupported-configuration — the policy is valid but asks for a capability this build/configuration cannot provide: a `[flows]` designation with no journal / no native backend, or `KEEL_BACKEND=native` with no native module. (Async effects inside a flow are supported — serialized in await order, per conformance/README.md's Tier 2 ordering rule — and no longer trigger this code.) Next: build the native module and make `.keel/` writable; `keel doctor`.
- KEEL-E010 attempts-exhausted — failed on the final permitted attempt; original error re-raised unchanged.
- KEEL-E011 timeout — exceeded the policy timeout.
- KEEL-E012 breaker-open — the breaker is open; the call failed fast, unattempted.
- KEEL-E013 rate-budget-exceeded — could not queue under the rate limit within the wait budget.
- KEEL-E014 non-idempotent-not-retried — a retryable failure on a non-idempotent call; observed, not retried (Level 0 hard rule). Add `idempotency = { header = "…" }` to make it retryable.
- KEEL-E015 non-retryable-error — error class not in `retry.on`; original re-raised.
- KEEL-E016 poll-deadline-exceeded — a poll-until-terminal call kept returning a pending status until `poll.deadline` ran out. Next: raise the deadline, or check that `until.field`/`until.terminal` name the response's real terminal signal. (The opposite failure — a poll that returns immediately and never loops — is usually the missing-field case: see `until.absent` above.)
- KEEL-E017 nested-sync-effect — a synchronous effect inside an open flow could not acquire the flow's step lock before the nested-effect deadline (30s by default). The most likely cause is nesting across OS threads: the thread-local re-entrancy guard can't see it, so the inner call would otherwise wait forever on a lock an outer effect of the same flow won't release until this one returns. Keel observes only that the lock stayed held, not who held it — a merely slow outer step is the other explanation. Only reachable inside an open flow (outside one, nesting across threads now just works). Next: call the inner effect from the same thread as the outer one, use the async path instead (it composes nesting), or move the nested call outside the wrapped effect — a FastAPI/Starlette `TestClient` suite hits this because the ASGI app runs in a portal thread inside the client's own intercepted request.
- KEEL-E020 cache-codec — a response could not be (de)serialized for the cache.
- KEEL-E030 flow-lease-held — the flow is being executed by another process (live lease).
- KEEL-E031 flow-nondeterminism — on replay the code diverged from the journal (or code changed). Set `flows.on_nondeterminism = "warn"|"branch"` to continue.
- KEEL-E032 flow-dead — the flow exhausted its resume-attempt cap (poison flow).
- KEEL-E033 cmd-side-effects-changed — a `cmd:` flow (or `keel exec`) refused to re-dispatch a failed command because its declared side-effect files changed since the last attempt. Next: inspect them, then `keel exec --force` or the durable, out-of-process `keel flows force <flow>`.
- KEEL-E040 internal — a Keel bug (invariant violation inside the core). File an issue with the trace id.

## DX invariants (tested in CI as behaviors)

1. Zero code changes in Python/TS (one optional attribute in Rust).
2. Uninstall = remove the package; code runs identically.
3. No daemon, no port, no login — state is files in `.keel/`.
4. Silence on success, precision on failure (what/why/next/trace).
5. Never swallow errors — the original propagates unchanged, with a `keel` attachment.
6. Everything has `--json` and stable exit codes.
7. Works offline — no telemetry, no phone-home.
8. Fast — `keel run` adds <100 ms startup; wrapping overhead ≤10 µs/call (measured ~0.8 µs, worst case, including the event sink and idempotency injection), published in the README.

## Determinism (for agents)

Identical inputs produce byte-identical `--json` (sorted keys, no wall-clock
timestamps unless asked). Suggestions are emitted as applyable diffs. Run
`keel doctor --json` before changing resilience behavior; `keel init --agents`
seeds `AGENTS.md` so future sessions inherit this context.

## Install

```
pip install keelrun keelrun-cli                # Python: library + CLI
npm install keelrun keelrun-cli                # Node: library + CLI
cargo add keelrun --rename keel                # Rust: library (#[keel::wrap])
cargo install keelrun-cli                      # Rust: CLI (cargo has no single command for both)
uvx --from keelrun-cli keel run app.py         # zero-install CLI, any language
```

Building from source (contributors):

```
maturin develop -m crates/keel-py/Cargo.toml   # native keel_core into the venv (Python)
pip install -e 'python/keel[dev]'
node node/keel/bin/keel-node-run.mjs app.mjs   # Node from-source `keel run`
cargo build -p keelrun-cli                      # the `keel` binary
```

## Conformance

58 scenarios in `conformance/scenarios/` (45 Tier 1, 13 Tier 2), run by the
real Rust core (all of them — Tier 2 additionally against a real Postgres
journal backend), the Rust/Python/Node stubs (every Tier 1 scenario; Tier 2
skipped by design — no journal), and the native front ends.
`conformance/README.md` is the normative semantics. Cross-language rules too
fine-grained for a scenario live in shared corpora under `conformance/`
(e.g. `operation_read/cases.json`, the referee for the Google operation-read
idempotency rule in all three front ends).
